Formulation:  
Amanda Jackson, a 19-year-old university student, presents with acute onset dysuria, increased urinary frequency, lower abdominal aching pain, and hematuria (pink urine). She has a history of IBS, which may contribute to abdominal symptoms but is less likely related to urinary complaints. The temporal relationship of symptoms and clinical presentation is consistent with acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection (cystitis). Sexual history raises the possibility of sexually transmitted infection (urethritis), which cannot be fully excluded despite absence of discharge or systemic symptoms. No red flag features (fever, flank pain, vomiting) are present indicating complications. Psychosocial factors include university life with moderate social support and recent experimentation with cannabis. Protective factors include insight and compliance willingness. Predisposing factors include female gender and sexual activity; precipitating factors include recent unprotected sexual intercourse; perpetuating factors are not evident.  

Mental Health Care Plan Details  

Principal Problem: Urinary tract infection (cystitis)  
- Patient Goal(s): Resolution of urinary symptoms, return to normal daily activities including university attendance  
- Clinical Goal(s): Confirm diagnosis with urine analysis, initiate effective antibiotic treatment, monitor symptom improvement, exclude complication or alternate diagnosis if symptoms persist  
- Actions (Patient): Provide urine sample as instructed, commence prescribed antibiotic therapy, maintain hydration, take analgesia as needed, report worsening symptoms (fever, back pain, vomiting) promptly  
- Actions (Clinician/GP): Provide prescription for appropriate antibiotic (Trimethoprim or Nitrofurantoin; dose/route/frequency not documented), arrange urine microscopy and culture, advise on symptom management, plan follow-up if symptoms do not improve in 7 days, offer guidance on STI screening if indicated  

Secondary Problem: Possible sexually transmitted infection (urethritis/cervicitis)  
- Patient Goal(s): Understand risks related to unprotected sex, prevent recurrence of symptoms  
- Clinical Goal(s): Assess for STI as required if symptoms persist or urine cultures negative, provide sexual health education and possible screening  
- Actions (Patient): Consider STI testing if recommended, practice safer sex measures including condom use  
- Actions (Clinician/GP): Provide advice on sexual health and contraception, arrange STI screening if clinically indicated, counsel regarding condom use  

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention:  
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered: urinary tract infection symptoms, importance of hydration, antibiotic use, signs of complications (fever, flank pain, vomiting), sexual health risks and condom use advised  
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening: Fever, flank or back pain, vomiting, persistent or worsening urinary symptoms  
- Coping Strategies: Hydration, analgesia (Paracetamol), timely medical review if symptoms worsen or fail to improve  

Consent, Coordination & Review:  
- Patient Consent to Plan: Implied by engagement and agreement in transcript  
- Copy of Mental Health Care Plan Given to Patient: Not recorded  
- Other Mental Health Professionals Involved in Patient Care: Not recorded  
- GP Acknowledgment (if completed by other MH Professional): Not applicable  
- Review Date: Advice to return if no improvement after one week; formal review date not recorded  

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)  
- Urinary tract infection (cystitis) — High likelihood; classic symptom constellation with no systemic signs indicating uncomplicated infection  
- Sexually transmitted infection (urethritis/cervicitis) — Medium likelihood; consistent with history of unprotected sex and symptoms despite absence of discharge  
- Urinary tract stone — Low likelihood; hematuria present but no flank pain or colicky symptoms  
- Interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome — Low likelihood; acute onset with hematuria less consistent with chronic non-infectious syndrome  
- Bladder or urethral neoplasm — Low likelihood; very rare at age 19 with acute symptom onset
